blocks.x: I mean just how it is.
Yeah well we want to get your name on here the first thing. Yeah. Could you tell us your full name? Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Include my middle name?
Yes if you don't mind.
Alright, let me get ready.
I'm ready.
You ready? Mm-hmm. Okay well my name is Charles Leopold Bockeyes.
You see?
And I am the youngest brother of the Bockeyes brothers.
See where's, what's the address here? I'd like to get the address.
2039 Turo.
I see and today's date is July the, hold on I forget. Do you know Herbie what the date is? You know?
Yes 18th eh? I think it's 18th.
It's Monday the 18th then huh?
Yeah Monday the 18th July. 1960.

Herbie what's your name? Herb Friedwald. Alright. And I'm Dick Allen then. Alright. We have the tape we're gonna play some of the old Piron records that you say you made years ago in New York. Is it ready? Yeah just about. Alright well we'll continue on talking for a minute. Could I get you a date of birth and place of birth?
Yes I was born in Algiers Louisiana. January the 14th 1900.
And uh, exactly what part of Algiers? You know the street?
Yeah I think it was on Powder Street. 530 Powder Street if hmm.
Uh huh. Interesting. You mentioned uh, several fellows in your family were musical?
Yes my daddy and uh, two brothers and also two sisters. Uh huh.
And what were their names?
Well I had one sister named Boetha and uh, Lillian. And my father was uh, Leopold Vorkaige. And of course my other two brothers is uh, Henry and Boethaige, Henry Clay and uh, Peter Boethaige.
Do you have any cousins that play?
Well I have one cousin in Algiers uh, that's a musician, Wilfred Boethaige and alto sax player.
Why don't we play one of the records now and you just tell us what you remember about them.
Well that's uh,
I think that's bouncing around eh? No, I don't think so. Who's that the box haven't you heard? This is New Orleans Wiggle. I'm thinking it's New Orleans Wiggle. That's it, yup. New Orleans Wiggle.
That's right. Well that number was written by my brother, Pete.
Who did he arrange it on?

He did his stuff. Pete wrote it and arranged it. And of course when it was in New York I think it was published by Williams. I'm not positive, I don't know, I'm sure it was. I know West Indies Blues was published by Clarence, you know. And uh, we did that number on uh, I think, OK recording. If I'm not mistaken. Because we did record for OK, the Brumvicks and Victor people. Three companies. Three companies. And uh, of course that's Teo that's clarinet you're hearing there. We had nine men in the orchestra and uh, according to the critics we had, considered one of the finest orchestras to hit New York at that time, you know. And uh, we played the uh, well it wasn't the Cotton Club then, it was Club Deluxe. It was owned by former heavyweight champion Jack Johnson and a man by the name of Levy. Then we played a one week's uh, tryout at Lafayette during the closing of the club for a redecoration period. And during that week we had critics who hit us, you see. And we had offers to go with uh, Joy's White Scandals. Which they torn down, the men didn't want to stay in New York. Also another big job in uh, a big summer resort I think it was in Bridgeport, Connecticut.
I heard you take a break back there on the banjo.
Yeah.
A little break. How much reading did you all do on a tune like that?

Well uh, we, we part of it was a bunch of gifted musicians. We practically memorized all those numbers. See? You know that that is the sport. We played them so many times. See? And we just memorized them. In fact we played a whole, a waterfall show without any music. All our own numbers. West Indies Blues was uh, a number thawed up by Pierron and uh, I don't know who else had anything to do with it. I sang it all the way through. In fact I was entertaining the band at all times. That's Mama's Gone Goodbye. Pete wrote that too. Him and Pierron I think.
I think he told me he wrote the music and Pierron wrote the words.
Yeah. Well Pierron was more of a lyric writer you see. Now Purple Rose I think it was, I'm not positive but I think it was more Pierron than Steele.
Really?
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Were these the tunes that you played on the job? Yeah.
Did you... That was our style. Yeah. Right there. Yeah.
That was our style, yeah, right there. We had a light band because we only had one trumpet and one trompon. Like now you have a low-ish brass section.
He was using a mute there.
Yeah.
Some kind of mute.
I don't think so.
He told me he didn't use a mute on that.

The system of recording was different than now, you know. You had to, the soloist had to get up and walk up to there. There was big microphones sticking out. You had to get so many feet from it. You know, sometimes it would be too much and sometimes it wasn't enough. And that's kind of difficult, you know. I think we was the first colored orchestra to play appointment and engagement at the Roseland. Fifty Fweys and Broadway. That was one of the most beautiful dance palettes in America at that time. And, uh...
Did you ever have a tryout for the George White Scandals show? Well, no, uh...

The George White Scandals. That's, I think I mentioned that. Mm-hmm. We did try out. But after trying out, the men didn't want to stay. Piron couldn't get them to stay. Up there, you know. Some of them had good jobs here. In fact, we were making lots of money here. We just went mostly on a trip. But then that was his greatest ambition was to reach the top. And in fact, it hurted him, you know, when the men actually turned him down. Cause he said he could have went to such great heights, you know. Had they would have stuck with him, you see. You know, we came back and back we had all the prominent work in New Orleans. New Orleans Country Club. Those debutantes and, uh, Carnival Balls and... Boston Club, Pickwick Club, Stratford Club. We had the cream of the work. And it got well paid for us. It was one of the reasons why the men wasn't too anxious to stay away from home. A lot of us was our first time away too, you see. Of course, I didn't have any sense of being the youngest member of the orchestra, you understand. But like my brother Pete, he was one of the key men. He for one got on sick. It was just one of those things, you know. It was a bad break. I understand that. It was a bad break for Pierron, I said it was. I think he would have went... We up that ladder there. He had the opportunity, you know. We were playing opposite an orchestra by the name of Mal Hallett. From Connecticut. At the Rhodeland. And during the time we turned on that George White Scandal deal. He said he would have cut his right arm off if he just could have got it. So, we turned the town, you see. Not we, I didn't see. Myself, because I didn't have much voice in the orchestra being just joined up with them when they left here, you see.
Were these other fellas longer than you?

Yeah. Every man in that band was older than me. I was the youngest member in the band. And I was 23 when we left here. We went up in 23 and we came back and went back in 24. We actually made two trips. The first time we played at the Cotton Club. And the second time we went to the Rosen's. Where Clines was negotiating with you see.
Do you remember any of the other bands that were active in New York at that time?

Well, there were a few of them up there. There was one band from Detroit, I think, was playing up there. Leroy, a fellow named Leroy Smith. A colored officer. He was out of Detroit. He actually was the man that put us wise through those fellas up there. You know, such as trying to hire your key men and break up your aggregation and things like that, you know. Did anybody try any of that with a fit-on band? Yeah, well we had several offers. I couldn't say it was that, but they tried to hire our men. Some white orchestras tried to hire me, my brother-in-law, Pete. And of course a number of other bands around there, you know.
Now did you say you knew that any of the men in the band played with other orchestras? Or didn't play with other orchestras?

I didn't know it. I never knew it to be a fact. Not no regular engagement. Unless they had jobs around doing a period when we wasn't doing anything. You know, they would hire to go play a one night gig or something like that. But I hardly think any of them played any regular engagement with anybody up there. If they did, I didn't know anything about it.
Well, didn't T.O. play with another band in New York at one time? Maybe later than that.
Well, T.O. went back to New York. He went back to New York in 32, I think. With my sister and that's where he died up there.
When did he die, man?

He died in 1930, I think. He was here and things were pretty rough here in the music business. You know, Paul Barbaran, I think. He came back and told him that he could get and wake up there. He was just crying for a man of his type. And he and my sister, they packed up and left. And that was the last I saw of him. I saw him when they brought him back, his body back. Where's he buried at? Where's he buried at? He buried in the St. Louis Cemetery. I guess when he is here.
Did he have a good reputation as a clarinetist in town?

Oh yeah, he was one of the finest they had here. In fact, his daddy was a clarinetist. His uncle, they were all great clarinetists. He was Mexican. He was Mexican, his father was. His mother was French. They tell me from way back to the great grandfathers, it was all clarinet players. He was actually a, he had one musician. He wasn't a little doubt about it.
He was a little bit of a big band. He was a little bit of a big band. He was a little bit of a big band. Do you know who he worked with?
What bands he worked with when he went back to New York?

No, I didn't know that because I stayed here. In fact, I don't think he did so well. Because he got desponding up there and got to drinking. I think it was part of his downfall, you know. Because Big Ord, you see, he taught such men as Big Ord. Albert Nicholas and this boy Simeon from Chicago was his scholar. And they all turned out to be great clarinet players, you see. So, when he got to New York, I learned that the, you know, fellas out here had helped him lean towards him and all. And that made him feel quite bad, you see. He was a great man, not only in music, he had a wonderful disposition. He was a good jazz clarinet player.
Did you say he was a good jazz clarinet player?
Yeah, he played jazz and he could play classics too. Play classics. He was just that type of man.
What about Pop-Pop? Did he play any jazz? Huh?

Well, Pop-Pop played a lot of that old Scott Joplin music, I would imagine, back then. You know, just before my time. You remember him? I remember him, yeah, but in retirement. I was a little bit of a fellow and I used to go around by. In fact, I started to take up the client at once under him. I guess about 15 years old. And I got disgusted, he was so strict. You know, young brother. I gave it up. I gave it up.
Is this bouncing around?
No, that's not. Yeah, I believe it is bouncing around. Mm-hmm. Did the younger T.O. ever play any of the Scott Joplin numbers?

Yeah, he played all that music. You see, back in those days, back in the... 1919, 1908, where the district was operating. A lot of cabarets. Most of those musicians played there. That's all they was playing back in those days, you know. That type of music. Big Ilui and Tiku and... All those men. Well, they're much older men than I am. Yet I knew them. Some of them I played with and... Some I never had to play the playing with. I knew them personally.
But you said you worked in the district yourself. You must have been working out.
No, I didn't work in the district. I played Tom Anderson on Ramport. When I was at the 10, I was just 19 years old.
Did you play any guitar or banjo at that time? No. Never had a lesson on anything?

I used to play guitar. You know, just by head like that. When I was a young kid. Sing and play. Just for past time. And then me and my daddy and my other brother, Henry. We used to play a little violin too. We had a little three piece band, you know. Played a lot of house poetry and things. And then I was always musical, you see. And then after I got married, Pete enticed me to take up the banjo, you see. Which I did. Made a start of the banjo and I... Went pretty good ways on the banjo. I don't say I was a great deal or so on them, but I held my aunt with some of the best we had around here. You know? I had an opportunity to stay in New York too, you know. Kiss me soon.
This is the one you used to sing on?
Yeah, I seen that woman in Poison Angel.
Yeah, yeah. Poison Angel. Poison Angel. My granddaughter. That's- That- Is the Pierron band the first regular band you worked with as a banjo player?
Yeah, yeah. First two-minute band, yeah. My granddaughter. That is, honey. Huh?
Now who were these singers? These were people in New York? Or did they travel with the band regularly?
No, that's Pierron and me. That's Pierron and you? It don't sound like it's on a real record. I don't know if it's... See, that's Pierron.
I didn't know that was you on the record. Yeah. I know they got another singer on the Sing West Indies Blues. I thought these were...
I sing that too. I'm the only man that did any singing with the band. Outside of Pierron, I helped out on this one record here. It's Kiss Me Sweet, you see.
Did you open a while Steve to sing any of his numbers?

Well, Steve used to do a lot of clowning, like, you know. He was more comedy type in the band, playing. Did Steve sing any of his numbers at Tranchinas? Well, he used to sing too, yeah, in between like that. After I joined the band, well, I took over the duties, you know.
What were some of the songs you sang with them?

Well, everything that was, you know, singable, I mean, including stock music and everything. Some original that they had music, like West Indies Blues. I made West Indies Blues. Do you remember who this is? No. I don't know, that's... That's a woman. That's a woman.
Peace you, huh? Yeah. I know it's not me. I made the original record myself. You know how I believe those things came about was maybe before we left here, you know.

I don't know. I don't know, that's... That's a woman. That's a woman. Peace you, huh? Yeah. I know it's not me. I made the original record myself. You know how I believe those things came about was maybe before we left here, you know. I don't know how she got on that.
She didn't work with the band regularly?
No. I don't remember her working with us at all. How she got on that record is beyond me.
Do you remember a woman named Leela Bolden? No. She's supposed to make some records with... Well, I guess I think it's just with Steve and Pierron. I'm not sure. I forget that.
No, I think it's supposed to be with the band.
No, I don't never remember this woman singing with us. With the orchestra, I mean. Mm-mm. That's a Pierron band, alright.
That's a Pierron band, alright. That would sound like us. I don't remember that record. How much of the drums could they record then?

Well, I don't know. It looked like during that time, the thing that was most effective on records was the cymbal. Because during the time we recorded, the only thing that the drummer would use would be the cymbal.
So they could use some wood blocks there for a while. Well, that's the wood block there, yeah. That's the wood block there, yeah.

That's the wood block there, yeah. That's the wood block there. I don't know. I don't know. I actually don't believe that's our orchestra. I don't know. I don't know. That's our orchestra. I don't remember that one recording with us at all. Because during the time we would record it, the only thing that the drummer would use would be the cymbal.
So they could use some wood blocks there for a while.
Well that's the wood block there, yeah. I don't know, I actually don't believe that's our orchestra. I don't remember that woman recording with us at all.
What it's supposed to be, I don't know.
Well it happened, it's beyond me. Unless it was something, full secret there. I know during the time I was with the orchestra, I did all that. West Indies Blues and all that.
Might be some other date or something, we'll have to look into that.

Unless, you know, maybe while it was up there, but even at that I can't remember. Now Lizzie Ma, this woman ever got with us. Did Lizzie Miles ever sing with you? No, Lizzie was singing down at the Capitol Palace on Lenox Avenue, down in the basement. At the time we was up there.
And you say the Piran Van was a pretty big success in the open?

Well, yes, I think we was 100%. And I think we would have been much greater if we'd have stayed, you know, and accepted such as that off him key circuit contract and all that we was offered, you know. And, uh, oh, he was very despondent. You see, he said that the fact that we thought the men would let him down, he would have stayed home. Yes, I felt. That was his life's ambition, you know.
Well, you once told me something about a tryout that you had. Huh? And, uh, you once told me something about a tryout the band had and Pete purposely didn't play well.

Oh, that was that, uh, George Weiss camp. You know. They didn't want to stay up there. The men didn't want to. They never was up away from home before. And then it looked like they understood they was just going for a trip. And after they got up there, well, opportunities began to present. They didn't want to accept, you see. They wanted to come back here. Of course, I came back with them. I didn't have no choice.
Did Pierron want to stay up there? Oh, yeah.

Like I told you, that was his ambition. To hit the top, you know. And he really had the chance. He really had. I give him credit. He had the chance. The door was wide open. He was a band that didn't want to stay up there. Didn't want to stay up there, that's all.
Before you started playing banjo, did they have saxophones here?

Well, they did have a saxophone. I understood that B. Shea was one of the first men to put a saxophone around there. That's before my time, you know. He was mostly clarinets back in those days. Well, this band must have added a saxophone pretty early.
Be wrong, man. Well, we had saxophones as far back as I can recollect.
I think it was... See, that was 23 when we went up there. And Louis was already playing sax then. Warning. Warning. He's been clarinet player too. Gunlaw was strictly clarinet player too.
Gunlaw was strictly clarinet player then he.

He began to switch over to the sax. He took up the tenor sax. And Warnick was playing the alto. See? So like I tell you, I'm only quoting the best I can remember because it's been so far back. I mean, it just got away from me a lot of that stuff, you know.
Did a Pierron band ever play what you call blues, low down blues, or anything like that? Yeah.

Yeah, we played blues whenever the occasion presented. We played a color dance or something, you know. We played a blues. Did you play many color dances? Well, not many. We was mostly a society band around here. Most of our work was with the society people. See?
But you would use a different style when you played for a colored audience?

No, we played all the same style. It's just that, yeah. Maybe the singing you changed your style of singing like that, you know. But the blues was something that was for the, those days, the most of the common people. That you played blues for, you know. Outside of St. Louis blues, but I'm talking about the real stomp down blues. You know, like when you played the economy all over the collaborators or places like that where, you know.
How was T.O. on the blues? It was fine.
Who were the outstanding blues players in the band? Well, I don't know.
Let me hear that. Now that sound more like the original record. Now that other record wasn't the original record.
No, it was a scratchy.
I knew it wasn't.
And we had to, you know, it changed us.
You hear, you hear the violin in there.
Did Pierron take a lot of solos himself?

Yeah. He... Yeah, that's the original, I reckon. We had another number we made. We had used it for the opening of our program in Vaudeville. Oh, that's it. Bright Star was the name. You ever heard that thing? That was a beautiful thing. Yeah. It was beautiful. Pete wrote that. Bright Star. That was a pretty number.
Is that the end of the music? Yeah, that's it.

Yeah, back in the day, as far as I can remember, I played with Bonnie Bigard and myself. Little Scram band, Buddy PT, you know, back in the... That band wasn't rated with these bands like this. I mean, they played... Just gig around, you know. Lot of colored work. For the white people, they played most of the poor class of people, you know.
Where did you work with Buddy PT?

All around. We used to go to Covington, Madisonville, and Ogilusa, all up and down that... Over there. And then we'd go to Hazel Hoist, Vicksburg, you know, and come back here and play. I think it was rough back in those days, man.
When was this? About what time?
Well, that was back around 1918, around then.
And what were you playing then? What instrument were you playing in Ireland, 1918?
I was playing the banjo then. I was playing the banjo.
Who led the band? The T? Was he the leader? What did...
The Find out who played in that band and stuff like that with Buddy Petit.

Yeah, I love playing with Buddy a while. In fact, I played with him a while and then I went with other little aggregations, you know, one night stands. Back those days, men would hire. They needed a guitar player or something. They just come and hire you, you know. I didn't keep no particular regular.

This boy Danny Small was, he was doing a dancing, a song and dance team. He would act with a girl by the name Ida Brown in the review. That's not Small's Paradise. That's not... No, not him. This boy was named Small, but he was an entertainer. And, uh... Well Frank said, uh, Danny took sick with indigestion and Frank says, Man, I only got 45 minutes before the show. He said, What I'm gonna do to fill out that spot? You know, oh man, he would know it was type of fill. He was going like that. So I said, uh, say Frank. I say you want me to...
